                    ### Question
                    A 30-year-old man comes to the physician because of an episode of bloody vomiting this morning and a 1-week history of burning upper abdominal pain. Two weeks ago, he sustained a head injury and was in a coma for 3 days. An endoscopy shows multiple, shallow hemorrhagic lesions predominantly in the gastric fundus and greater curvature. Biopsies show patchy loss of epithelium and an acute inflammatory infiltrate in the lamina propria that does not extend beyond the muscularis mucosa. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Type B gastritis
opb. Dieulafoy lesion
opc. Cushing ulcer
opd. Penetrating ulcer
ope. Erosive gastritis

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with bloody vomiting and burning upper abdominal pain, alongside a recent head injury and coma, which suggests the possibility of stress-related mucosal disease. Endoscopy reveals shallow hemorrhagic lesions primarily in the gastric fundus, and biopsy findings show patchy loss of epithelium with acute inflammatory infiltrate limited to the lamina propria, not extending beyond the muscularis mucosa. This presentation is consistent with erosive gastritis, particularly given the context of the head injury. Cushing ulcers, while a consideration due to the head injury, typically penetrate deeper than the muscularis mucosa, which is not the case here. Therefore, the most likely diagnosis is erosive gastritis.
